subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Lower GI Bleeding and Motility: Hirschsprung, Meckel, and Coeliac

steps.tx: Evacuation of dark mucus mixed with sloughed necrotic mucosal elements heralds serious pediatric bowel ischaemia. Classically associated with late ileocolic intussusception, passing **red currant jelly stool** occurs when severe mesenteric venous thrombosis leads to mucosal infarction. Any infant presenting with this finding mandates urgent resuscitation, surgical consultation, and immediate diagnostic imaging to assess bowel viability.
steps.say: Red currant jelly stool consists of sloughed bowel mucosa, blood, and mucus from severe venous infarction. It signifies advanced intussusception requiring urgent surgical evaluation.

left.title: Pathophysiology of Currant Stool
points: Mesenteric vessel compression in intussuscipiens
Severe venous engorgement and capillary rupture
Sloughing of ischaemic enterocytes and goblet mucus
Evacuated per rectum as gelatinous red mass

right.title: Immediate Clinical Actions
points: Establish wide-bore intravenous access
Initiate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
Decompress stomach with nasogastric tube
Prepare for emergency surgical exploration

steps.tx: Congenital failure of neural crest craniocaudal migration arrests intrinsic enteric autonomic innervation. In neonates with **Hirschsprung disease**, absent ganglion cells in both the myenteric Auerbach and submucosal Meissner plexuses result in an unrelaxed, spastic aganglionic colonic segment. The disease predominantly affects the rectosigmoid junction in eighty percent of cases, presenting with delayed meconium passage.
steps.say: Hirschsprung disease arises from arrested neural crest migration, leaving the rectum devoid of ganglion cells. Eighty percent of cases involve the rectosigmoid colon.

vis.alt: Barium enema radiograph showing narrowed distal aganglionic rectosigmoid and dilated proximal colon transition zone.
vis.caption: Contrast enema highlighting the cone-shaped transition zone between narrowed rectum and dilated proximal colon. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Delayed meconium passage beyond the first forty-eight hours of life raises immediate suspicion of colonic aganglionosis. Ninety percent of healthy term neonates pass meconium within twenty-four hours; delay signifies **neonatal intestinal aganglionosis**. Digital rectal examination produces a pathognomonic explosive discharge of retained flatus and liquid faeces, termed the blast sign or squirt sign, alongside progressive abdominal distension and bilious emesis.
steps.say: Failure to pass meconium within forty-eight hours suggests Hirschsprung disease. Digital rectal examination triggers an explosive expulsion of liquid stool and gas.

rows: No meconium by 48 hours in term infant
Squirt sign / Blast sign on finger withdrawal
Must sample at least 2 cm above dentate line

steps.tx: The most catastrophic complication of congenital aganglionic megacolon carries substantial infant mortality. Rapid bacterial overgrowth and mucosal translocation trigger **Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis** (HAEC), presenting with explosive foul-smelling diarrhoea, abdominal distension, fever, and rapid septic shock. Management requires urgent rectal irrigation with warm isotonic saline, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and emergency diverting stoma if clinical deterioration occurs.
steps.say: Hirschsprung enterocolitis presents with explosive foul-smelling diarrhea, toxic distension, and sepsis. Immediate saline rectal washouts and intravenous antibiotics are life-saving.

left.title: Hirschsprung Enterocolitis Signs
points: Sudden explosive watery diarrhoea and lethargy
Severe tender abdominal distension
Metabolic acidosis and septic shock
Leukocytosis with prominent band forms

right.title: Emergency Treatment Protocol
points: Repeated rectal washouts using large-bore catheter
Instil warm isotonic saline to decompress bowel
Start IV ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole
Perform emergency leveling colostomy if refractory

steps.tx: Incomplete obliteration of the embryonic vitellointestinal duct produces the most common congenital gastrointestinal anomaly. A classic **Meckel diverticulum** represents a true diverticulum containing all three bowel wall layers on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. It follows the rule of twos: occurring in two percent of the population, located two feet proximal to the ileocaecal valve, and measuring two inches in length.
steps.say: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital bowel anomaly, following the rule of twos. It arises from the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum.

rows: Male to female ratio 2:1 in symptomatic cases
Arises on antimesenteric border of ileum
Gastric mucosa in 60-80% of bleeding cases

steps.tx: Ectopic gastric acid secretion provokes peptic ulceration of adjacent normal ileal mucosa lacking acid-protective mechanisms. Children under two years present with painless, profuse **lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage**, passing brick-red or maroon-coloured melenic stools without abdominal tenderness. Diagnosis is established by Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel scan), which is avidly taken up by heterotopic gastric parietal cells, showing a focal right lower quadrant hotspot.
steps.say: Heterotopic gastric mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates adjacent ileum, causing painless massive rectal bleeding. A pertechnetate scan confirms the diagnosis.

left.title: Meckel Diverticulum Presentation
points: Painless massive rectal bleeding in toddler
Passing brick-red or dark maroon stools
Absence of preceding abdominal colic or fever
Severe microcytic anaemia or hypovolaemic shock

right.title: Technetium-99m Scintigraphy (Meckel Scan)
points: Pertechnetate accumulates in gastric mucosa
Synchronous uptake with stomach wall
Pretreatment with H2 blockers enhances uptake
Laparoscopy indicated if scintigraphy is negative

steps.tx: A hot spot low in the right abdomen on this scan is stomach tissue in the wrong organ. A **Meckel diverticulum** holding ectopic gastric mucosa takes up pertechnetate just as the stomach does, because the tracer targets mucus secreting cells. That uptake explains painless heavy bleeding in a toddler: acid from the patch ulcerates neighbouring ileum. A negative scan never fully excludes the lesion when the story is strong.
steps.say: Pertechnetate concentrates in ectopic gastric mucosa inside a Meckel diverticulum, marking the bleeding source in a toddler. A negative scan cannot fully exclude it.

vis.alt: Technetium pertechnetate scan showing focal right lower quadrant uptake in a Meckel diverticulum.
vis.caption: A focal hot spot glows in the right lower abdomen where ectopic gastric mucosa lines a diverticulum. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten ingestion affects genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. In infants receiving wheat-based weaning foods, **pediatric coeliac disease** typically manifests between nine and twenty-four months of age with chronic malabsorptive diarrhoea, failure to thrive, abdominal distension, marked muscle wasting, anorexia, and apathy. Secondary lactose intolerance and nutritional deficiencies are common.
steps.say: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten in wheat, rye, and barley. Weaned infants present with chronic diarrhea, distension, and poor growth.

rows: Normal crypt depth and villous height
Marked IELs, crypt hyperplasia, villous atrophy
Diagnostic gold standard for active coeliac disease

steps.tx: Serological screening guides definitive confirmation and long-term surveillance in suspected coeliac disease. First-line screening utilizes serum **anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies**, which demonstrate over ninety-five percent sensitivity and specificity. Because selective IgA deficiency occurs ten times more frequently in coeliac patients, total serum IgA must be measured concurrently, switching to IgG-based testing if IgA deficiency is confirmed.
steps.say: Measure anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA along with total serum IgA for coeliac screening. Endoscopic duodenal biopsy confirms Marsh type three villous atrophy.

left.title: Diagnostic Serological Panel
points: Anti-tTG IgA is the preferred first-line test
Anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) for confirmation
Total serum IgA rules out selective IgA deficiency
IgG-deamidated gliadin peptides in IgA deficiency

right.title: Lifelong Dietary Management
points: Strict elimination of wheat, rye, and barley
Gluten-free oats tolerated by most children
Nutritional recovery and villous regeneration in 6 months
Antibody levels normalize within one year of diet
